Photo by Gregory Cooper, NLR 97442 Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 | 37 Molecular Simulations Improve Water Purification Membranes Reverse osmosis membranes are widely used for desalination and water purification, yet their frequent deformation under compaction reduces water flow and limits the membranes’ filtering capacity. Supported by the National Alliance for Water Innovation (NAWI) and funded by DOE’s CMEI, researchers use molecular modeling to understand how ultrahigh pressures change membrane structure and how improved designs can prevent this deformation. Large-scale molecular simulations enabled by Kestrel allowed the team to visualize, at the atomic level, how pressure and water flow can compress individual membrane layers. These insights revealed how even small structural shifts can restrict water throughput, raising energy costs for clean water production. Building on this knowledge, researchers identified a robust membrane design that resists physical compaction while maintaining over 99% salt rejection and limiting water permeability loss to under 10% at pressures up to 200 bar. Published in Nature Communications,17 this work demonstrates how molecular-level understanding can lead to more durable, longer-lasting desalination membranes. By maintaining performance under demanding conditions, these new membranes could reduce operating costs, improve industrial reliability, and expand access to clean water in regions facing increasing water stress. Photo by Getty Images 1450419288 17 https://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63639-0 38 | Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 Advanced Computing Annual Report 2025 | 39 Understanding Alternative Aviation-Fuel Behavior for Scale-Up It is essential to understand how fuels behave under the extreme conditions inside modern jet engines. With funding from CMEI, researchers are developing high-fidelity simulation tools to study how changes in fuel properties influence spray breakup, flame stabilization, and lean blowout behavior—key factors that determine engine efficiency and reliability. Using large-scale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and turbulence-resolving simulations, the team can capture complex multiphase flow physics with up to 21 million computational cells, a scale made possible by Kestrel. These simulations reveal how variation in droplet size alters flame spread, anchoring location, and local fuel-air mixing while still maintaining similar global combustion behavior. Recently featured in the Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power,18 this modeling capability improves researchers’ ability to predict how change in fuel atomization influences stability, efficiency, and performance in real jet engines.
